lessons.title: Principles of security operations
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of two gears turning together, one marked with a padlock, the other with a wrench: security day to day.
objectives: Apply separation of duties, job rotation, mandatory vacation and dual control.
Describe a change management process, including in an emergency.
Explain the role of configuration baselines and of the asset inventory.

references.title: ISO/IEC 27002:2022, controls 5.3 (segregation of duties), 5.9 (inventory of assets), 8.9 (configuration management) and 8.32 (change management)

blocks.text: Security day to day

Security operations cover everything that keeps security running every day: controlling the people who act on systems, governing changes, knowing your assets and configurations, monitoring and reacting. A perfect policy is useless if these daily actions are not carried out.
Controls on people

rows: A sensitive task is split between several people
Fraud carried out alone (creating a supplier AND paying it)
Two people must act together, at the same time
A lone action on a critical asset (master key, safe)
Long-running fraud and dependence on a single person
Required absence of several consecutive days
Fraud that needs daily presence to stay hidden
The damage from a compromised account or a mistake

blocks.title: Key point
blocks.text: Separation of duties forces collusion in order to commit fraud: two people have to agree. Job rotation and mandatory vacation, for their part, mainly serve to DETECT fraud that is already in place.
"Separate to prevent, rotate to discover." Separation of duties and dual control = preventive; rotation and mandatory vacation = detective.
Change management

blocks.title: The path of a change
blocks.alt: Six-step diagram: change request, impact and risk analysis, approval by the change advisory board, testing and rollback plan, implementation during a planned window, review and documentation update.

blocks.title: Emergency change (changement d'urgence)
blocks.text: Change applied without waiting for the normal process, for example to fix an exploited flaw. It is still tracked, approved by an authorized person, then regularized and reviewed afterward.

In the SOC, an undeclared change often looks like an attack: a newly opened port, a service account created, a firewall rule modified. The change calendar is one of the first documents to check during triage.
Configurations and assets

blocks.title: Configuration baseline (configuration de référence)
blocks.text: Approved and documented configuration state of a system, used as a point of comparison. Any deviation (drift) must be explained by an approved change.

blocks.title: Asset inventory (inventaire des actifs)
blocks.text: Up-to-date list of hardware, software, data and services, with their owner and criticality. You cannot protect what you do not know.

blocks.title: Good practices
items: Harden systems from a recognized guide, then freeze that configuration as the baseline.
Automatically detect configuration drift and match it against approved changes.
Reconcile the asset inventory with what the network, the EDR and the SIEM see: an unknown workstation is an alert.
Plan a rollback for every significant change.

blocks.title: Shadow IT (informatique de l'ombre)
blocks.text: A server or cloud service set up outside official channels is neither inventoried, nor patched, nor monitored. It is a classic entry point for an attacker.

blocks.title: SOC case: the port that opens at night
blocks.text: At 2:10 a.m., the L1 analyst sees a server exposing a new administration port. The analyst checks the change calendar: no change planned. The alert is escalated to L2, who discovers that a contractor changed the configuration without a request. It was not an attack, but the deviation is handled as an incident: return to the baseline, reminder of the process to the contractor, and a new rule to detect drift.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: change management is my first safety net against mistakes and backdoors.
SOC manager: without a change calendar, my analysts lose hours on false alerts.
Auditor: I take a sample of changes and check the request, approval, test and review.
Risk manager: an asset missing from the inventory is a risk that has never been assessed.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Separation of duties (two people for two steps) ≠ dual control (two people at the same time for one action).
Job rotation and mandatory vacation are mainly DETECTIVE controls.
An emergency change does not escape the process: it is regularized afterward.
Collusion is the weak point of separation of duties.
Controls on people: separation of duties, dual control, rotation, mandatory vacation, least privilege.
Change management: request, analysis, approval, test, implementation, review.
Configuration baseline and asset inventory: know in order to protect and detect deviations.

lessons.title: Logging and SIEM
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a funnel: at the top, many small sheets of logs; at the bottom, a single alert bell.
objectives: Choose what to log and protect the logs (clock, integrity, retention).
Describe how a SIEM works, from collection to alert.
Tell apart true and false positives, true and false negatives.
Place UEBA and SOAR in relation to the SIEM.

references.title: NIST SP 800-92, Guide to Computer Security Log Management

blocks.text: Logging well

A log is the record of an event: a login, a command, a change of rights, a blocked file. Without logs, there is no investigation, no detection and no evidence. But logging everything, without sorting, drowns the useful information and is expensive.

blocks.title: What to log first
items: Successful and failed authentications, especially on privileged accounts and remote access.
Creation, deletion and modification of accounts, groups and rights.
Configuration changes and shutdowns of security services (antivirus, EDR, logging itself).
Access to sensitive data and large exports.
Network traffic at the boundaries: firewall, proxy, DNS, VPN.

blocks.title: Three conditions for a log to be useful
blocks.text: 1. Clocks are synchronized (NTP), otherwise a timeline cannot be rebuilt. 2. Logs are protected against modification (central forwarding, write-once storage, hashes). 3. The retention period is defined, according to investigation needs and legal obligations.
"Time, Integrity, Retention": a log with the wrong time, that can be modified or that is deleted too early proves nothing.
The SIEM, from collection to alert

blocks.title: The path of an event through a SIEM
blocks.alt: Five-step diagram: log collection, normalization into a common format, enrichment with context, correlation according to rules, alert sent to the SOC for triage.

blocks.title: SIEM, Security Information and Event Management (gestion des informations et des événements de sécurité)
blocks.text: Platform that centralizes logs, normalizes them, correlates them and produces alerts. It is also used to search the history and keep records for investigations.

blocks.title: Correlation (corrélation)
blocks.text: Linking several events, sometimes from different sources, to recognize a scenario. Example: ten failures then a success on the same account, followed by a VPN connection from a new country.
Good alert or false alert?

blocks.title: The four outcomes of a detection
blocks.alt: Two-by-two grid. Real attack without an alert: false negative, the most dangerous. Real attack with an alert: true positive. No attack and no alert: true negative. No attack but an alert: false positive, which wears analysts out.

blocks.text: A SOC that receives thousands of false positives ends up ignoring the real ones. Tuning a rule is not a weakness: it is what makes alerts credible. But be careful, tuning that is too strict creates false negatives.
Around the SIEM

rows: Analysis of user and machine behavior, detection of deviations from the usual
An accountant who suddenly downloads 10 GB at 3 a.m.
Orchestration and automation of the response, using playbooks
Isolate a workstation and block an address as soon as an alert is confirmed
Detection and response on endpoints (EDR), extended to several sources (XDR)
Stop a suspicious encryption process on a workstation

blocks.title: Erased logs
blocks.text: An attacker who obtains administration rights often tries to erase local logs to hide their tracks. Real-time forwarding to a central SIEM, and an alert when logs are cleared, defeat this technique.

blocks.title: SOC case: the clock that runs late
blocks.text: During an investigation, the team rebuilds the timeline of an intrusion. The firewall logs place the suspicious connection at 2:02 p.m., the server logs at 1:55 p.m.: the server was no longer synchronized. It takes hours to realign the events. Measures taken: NTP mandatory on all systems, an alert on clock drift, and a check of each source's time when it is connected to the SIEM.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I fund the SIEM to detect fast, not to store terabytes that nobody reads.
SOC manager: every rule must have a purpose, a handling procedure and a tracked false-positive rate.
Auditor: I check the retention period, the protection of logs and clock synchronization.
Risk manager: a false negative on a critical scenario is a residual risk to document.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: False positive = alert without an attack; false negative = attack without an alert (the most dangerous).
The SIEM detects and correlates; SOAR automates the response.
Without clock synchronization, correlation and the timeline are distorted.
Logs must have their integrity protected: a log that can be modified has no value as evidence.
Log what is useful: authentications, rights, configuration, sensitive data, network boundaries.
Synchronized time, protected integrity, defined retention.
SIEM: collection, normalization, enrichment, correlation, alert.
True/false positive, true/false negative; UEBA, SOAR, EDR/XDR around the SIEM.

lessons.title: The SOC: organization, triage, hunting and indicators
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a monitoring desk with three screens: a curve, a map and a red alert, with a headset in front.
objectives: Describe how a SOC is organized (levels 1, 2 and 3) and its roles.
Carry out the triage of an alert with a playbook.
Tell apart IOC and IOA, and place threat hunting and MITRE ATT&CK.
Monitor a SOC with indicators such as MTTD and MTTR.

references.title: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, Incident Response Recommendations and Considerations for Cybersecurity Risk Management
MITRE ATT&CK, knowledge base of attack tactics and techniques

blocks.text: How a SOC is organized

blocks.title: The path of an alert
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: the alert arrives, the level 1 analyst sorts and qualifies it, the level 2 analyst investigates and contains, level 3 handles complex cases, hunting and detection engineering.
blocks.text: Around them: the detection engineer (rules), the threat intelligence analyst (CTI) and the SOC manager.

blocks.title: Triage
blocks.text: First analysis of an alert: is it founded, how severe is it, should it be escalated? Triage relies on context (asset, user, history) and on a playbook.

blocks.title: Playbook, also called runbook
blocks.text: Written procedure that describes step by step how to handle a type of alert: checks, decisions, containment actions, people to notify. It makes handling fast and consistent.
The 3 triage questions: "Is it real? Is it serious? Who do I hand it over to?"
Detecting better: indicators and hunting

rows: Trace of an attack that is already known
Hash of a malicious file, IP address of a command server
Behavior that reveals an ongoing attack, whatever the tool
A word processor that launches a command interpreter
Proactive search, starting from a hypothesis, for attacks that the alerts did not see
"Is an attacker using scheduled tasks to persist?"
Public base of tactics and techniques observed among attackers
Measure which techniques our rules cover

blocks.title: Key point
blocks.text: An IOC (address, hash) is easy to change: the attacker changes address in a few minutes. A behavior (IOA, ATT&CK technique) is much harder for them to change. Detecting behaviors hinders the attacker more.
Hunting starts with a hypothesis, not with an alert. If the hunt finds something, a new detection rule is derived from it: that is how the SOC improves.
Steering a SOC

blocks.title: Average SOC times (example)
blocks.alt: Bar chart with example figures: mean time to detect 6 hours, mean time to qualify 1 hour, mean time to respond 4 hours.
blocks.text: Example figures. MTTD: mean time between the start of an incident and its detection. MTTR: mean time to respond to it (contain and remediate). The lower they go, the better.

blocks.title: Other useful indicators
items: False-positive rate per rule, to know what to tune.
Coverage of the priority ATT&CK techniques by at least one tested rule.
Share of critical sources connected to the SIEM without collection gaps.
Number of pending alerts and time to pick them up.

blocks.title: Alert fatigue
blocks.text: Too many unreliable alerts exhaust analysts: they work fast, skip steps, and a real attack goes unnoticed. Tuning, automation and task rotation are the remedies.

blocks.title: SOC case: the macro that launches PowerShell
blocks.text: The EDR reports that a word-processing document launched PowerShell on an assistant's workstation. The L1 applies the "execution from a document" playbook: checks the email sender, the file hash and the outbound connections. The connection to an unknown address confirms the alert. The L1 isolates the workstation through the EDR and escalates to L2, who finds the same email in 12 other mailboxes, deletes it everywhere and blocks the domain. L3 turns the case into a hunting rule on the matching ATT&CK technique.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I track MTTD and MTTR every month and compare them with the targets set with management.
SOC manager: my playbooks are reviewed after every significant incident.
Auditor: I check that every critical alert was handled, with a timestamp and a decision.
Risk manager: the SOC shortens incidents, and therefore their impact; it is a detective and corrective control.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: IOC = known trace (address, hash); IOA = attack behavior.
Threat hunting is proactive and starts from a hypothesis; triage reacts to an alert.
MTTD measures detection, MTTR the response.
The SOC is mainly a detective control, with a corrective part (containment).
L1 sorts, L2 investigates and contains, L3 handles the complex cases, hunts and improves detection.
Playbooks for fast and consistent handling.
IOC, IOA, threat hunting, MITRE ATT&CK.
Indicators: MTTD, MTTR, false positives, coverage, connected sources.

questions.prompt: In a company, the same person can create a supplier and approve its payment. Which principle is not being followed?
choices: Need to know
Defense in depth
Separation of duties
Job rotation
questions.explanation: Splitting sensitive steps among several people prevents fraud committed by one person alone: this is separation of duties.

whyNot.0: Need to know concerns access to information.
whyNot.1: Defense in depth stacks layers of technical and organizational protection.
whyNot.3: Rotation moves people between positions; it does not split the steps.

questions.prompt: Which control mainly serves to DETECT a fraud that requires its perpetrator to be present every day?
choices: Mandatory vacations
Separation of duties
Least privilege
Dual control
questions.explanation: During mandatory leave, a replacement takes over the position and may discover the anomalies.

whyNot.1: Separation of duties is mainly preventive.
whyNot.2: Least privilege limits rights; it does not reveal fraud.
whyNot.3: Dual control is preventive: two people act together.

questions.prompt: Opening the encryption key safe requires two people present at the same time, each with their own code. What is this control called?
choices: Need to know
Dual control (two-person control)
Job rotation
Separation of duties
questions.explanation: Two people must act together, at the same moment, on the same action: this is dual control.

whyNot.0: Need to know limits access to information.
whyNot.2: Rotation moves people between positions over time.
whyNot.3: Separation of duties assigns different steps to different people.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of separation of duties?
choices: Collusion between several people
It is prohibited by ISO/IEC 27001
It requires vacations
It prevents any delegation
questions.explanation: If the people involved agree among themselves, they can get around the control: this is collusion.

whyNot.1: Separation of duties is, on the contrary, a recommended measure.
whyNot.2: Mandatory vacations are a different measure.
whyNot.3: It frames delegation without prohibiting it.

questions.prompt: Which step must come before implementing a major change in production?
choices: Deleting the server's old logs
Disabling the antivirus to avoid blockages
Informing customers once the change is complete
Impact analysis, approval and a rollback plan
questions.explanation: A controlled change is analyzed, approved and tested, with a way to roll back.

whyNot.1: Disabling the antivirus weakens security.
whyNot.2: Informing after the fact does not replace prior approval.

questions.prompt: An actively exploited flaw requires an immediate fix, without waiting for the next change board meeting. What should be done?
choices: Fix it directly in production, with no ticket or record, to go faster
Wait for the next change advisory board meeting despite the exploitation
Let each administrator decide alone, based on their own assessment
Apply an emergency change approved by an authorized person, recorded, then reviewed afterward
questions.explanation: The emergency change is fast-tracked but remains approved, recorded and regularized.

whyNot.0: An unrecorded change breaks change management and complicates investigations.
whyNot.1: Waiting lets the exploitation continue.
whyNot.2: An isolated, uncontrolled decision creates a risk of error and malicious action.

questions.prompt: A tool compares the configuration of the servers to their approved state every night and reports any differences. Which concept is being used?
choices: An internal penetration test run every night
A quantitative risk analysis based on ALE
A business continuity plan and its failover tests
A baseline configuration and drift detection
questions.explanation: The baseline configuration is the approved state; any difference (drift) must match an authorized change.

whyNot.0: A penetration test simulates a one-off attack.
whyNot.1: Quantitative analysis puts figures on risks.
whyNot.2: The continuity plan aims at resuming business.

questions.prompt: Why is the asset inventory a prerequisite for security operations?
choices: Because you cannot protect or monitor what you do not know about
Because it automatically encrypts the assets' data
Because it replaces the firewall for the listed assets
Because it removes the vulnerabilities of the listed systems
questions.explanation: Without an inventory, systems are left without patches, without monitoring and without an owner.

whyNot.1: The inventory does not encrypt anything.
whyNot.2: The inventory does not filter any traffic.
whyNot.3: The inventory helps find vulnerabilities; it does not remove them.

questions.prompt: Which of these controls are mainly DETECTIVE? (2 answers)
choices: Job rotation
Mandatory vacations
Dual control
Separation of duties
questions.explanation: Rotation and mandatory vacations bring another person into the position, who may discover a fraud.

whyNot.2: Dual control prevents a person from acting alone: it is preventive.
whyNot.3: Separation of duties prevents fraud by one person: it is preventive.

questions.prompt: The SOC discovers an unknown server, installed by a business team and exposed to the Internet. Which actions are the priority? (2 answers)
choices: Immediately delete all its data without telling anyone
Check its exposure and vulnerabilities, then connect it to monitoring
Identify it and add it to the inventory with an owner
Ignore it since it is not official
questions.explanation: A shadow asset must be known, assessed and monitored; the decision to keep or remove it is made afterward with its owner.

whyNot.0: A sudden deletion can destroy business data and evidence.
whyNot.3: Ignoring it leaves a door open.

questions.prompt: Why must the clocks (NTP) of all systems that produce logs be synchronized?
choices: To encrypt the logs with a time-based key
To speed up traffic on the internal network
To be able to correlate events and rebuild a reliable timeline
To reduce the volume of logs stored in the SIEM
questions.explanation: Clocks that are out of sync distort correlation and the timeline of an investigation.

whyNot.1: Synchronization does not speed up the network.
whyNot.3: The volume does not depend on the time.

questions.prompt: A real attack takes place, but no alert is raised. What is this?
choices: A false negative
A true negative
A true positive
A false positive
questions.explanation: An undetected attack is a false negative: it is the most dangerous case.

whyNot.1: A true negative is the absence of an alert when there is no attack.
whyNot.2: A true positive is a correctly detected attack.
whyNot.3: A false positive is an alert with no attack.

questions.prompt: A rule generates 300 alerts a day, 299 of which concern a legitimate backup tool. What is the problem and the right response?
choices: True positives; immediately isolate the backup server
False positives; tune the rule in a documented way
True negatives; change nothing, the rule works as intended
False negatives; delete the rule to reduce the noise
questions.explanation: Alerts with no attack are false positives; the rule is tuned in a documented way, not deleted.

whyNot.0: The tool is legitimate: isolating the server would be a mistake.
whyNot.2: Useless alerts wear analysts out: action is needed.
whyNot.3: These are extra alerts, not missed attacks; deleting the rule would create false negatives.

questions.prompt: In a SIEM, which step converts logs in different formats into a common format?
choices: Encryption
Correlation
Archiving
Normalization
questions.explanation: Normalization puts the fields (date, user, address) into a common format to allow searching and correlation.

whyNot.1: Correlation links events that have already been normalized.
whyNot.2: Archiving retains the logs.

questions.prompt: Which measure best protects the logs against a malicious administrator who wants to erase their tracks?
choices: Compress and archive the logs every night on the same server
Keep the logs only on the local server, with rights restricted to the administrator
Reduce the retention period to 24 hours to limit exposure
Send them in real time to a centralized SIEM, on immutable storage, managed by another team
questions.explanation: Immediate centralization, separation of duties and write-once storage preserve the integrity of the logs.

whyNot.0: Compression does not protect against modification.
whyNot.1: A local administrator can erase local logs.
whyNot.2: Short retention destroys useful evidence.

questions.prompt: Which statements about SOAR are correct? (2 answers)
choices: It orchestrates several tools (EDR, firewall, email)
It makes analysts unnecessary
It automates response actions using playbooks
It replaces logging
questions.explanation: SOAR orchestrates the tools and automates repetitive response tasks; analysts keep the decision on complex cases.

whyNot.1: It relieves analysts but does not replace them.
whyNot.3: SOAR relies on alerts and logs; it does not replace them.

questions.prompt: A tool reports that an accountant is downloading 10 GB of data at 3 a.m. for the first time. What type of analysis produced this alert?
choices: Antivirus signature analysis on the workstation
User and entity behavior analytics (UEBA)
A test restore of the night's backups
An authenticated vulnerability scan of the workstation
questions.explanation: UEBA learns the usual behavior and reports significant deviations.

whyNot.0: A signature recognizes a known file, not unusual behavior.
whyNot.2: A restore test checks the backups.
whyNot.3: A vulnerability scan looks for flaws.

questions.prompt: Which event is the MOST important to log and monitor?
choices: Printing a test page on a network printer
Adding an account to the domain administrators group
Opening the Start menu on a workstation
A user changing their desktop wallpaper
questions.explanation: Changes to privileged accounts and groups are critical security events.

whyNot.0: A test page is not a critical event.
whyNot.2: This event has no security value.
whyNot.3: The wallpaper has no security value.

questions.prompt: Which conditions give a log evidential value during an investigation? (2 answers)
choices: Integrity protection (immutable storage, hashes)
Reliable timestamps, from synchronized clocks
A proprietary file format
A different color for each source
questions.explanation: A reliable log must be correctly dated and must not have been modifiable.

whyNot.2: The format provides no guarantee of integrity.
whyNot.3: The display has no effect on evidential value.

questions.prompt: Which correlation rule is the most relevant for detecting a compromised account?
choices: An alert for every successful logon, whatever the account
An alert for every scheduled restart of a production server
Several failures, one success, then a logon from an unusual country
An alert for every print job started by a user
questions.explanation: Correlation combines several weak signals to recognize a credible scenario.

whyNot.0: One alert per logon would produce a flood of false positives.
whyNot.1: A scheduled restart is expected.
whyNot.3: Print jobs do not signal an account compromise.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of a level 1 SOC analyst?
choices: Developing and testing business applications
Negotiating the company's cyber insurance contracts
Triaging and qualifying alerts, then escalating if needed
Writing the security policy and getting it approved
questions.explanation: Level 1 receives the alerts, checks whether they are founded, assesses their severity and escalates.

whyNot.0: Development is not a SOC mission.
whyNot.1: Insurance falls under risk management.
whyNot.3: The policy falls under governance (CISO, executive management).

questions.prompt: What does MTTD measure?
choices: The number of rules in the SIEM
The log retention period
The average time to restore a backup
The average time between the start of an incident and its detection
questions.explanation: MTTD (Mean Time To Detect): the average time to detect an incident.

whyNot.0: The number of rules is not a time.
whyNot.1: Retention is a storage period, not a detection time.
whyNot.2: Restoring falls under continuity; the response time is the MTTR.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an indicator of attack (IOA) rather than an indicator of compromise (IOC)?
choices: A word processor that launches a command interpreter
The IP address of a known command server
The SHA-256 hash of a known malicious file
A malicious domain name listed by a vendor
questions.explanation: An IOA describes attack behavior, independent of the tool used; the others are known traces (IOCs).

whyNot.1: A known address is an IOC.
whyNot.2: A known hash is an IOC.
whyNot.3: A listed domain is an IOC.

questions.prompt: What characterizes threat hunting?
choices: A proactive, hypothesis-driven search for undetected attacks
An annual compliance audit run by an outside firm
Buying lists of malicious addresses from a vendor
Handling SIEM alerts in the order they arrive
questions.explanation: Hunting starts from a hypothesis and actively looks for what the alerts missed.

whyNot.1: An audit checks compliance; it does not look for an attacker.
whyNot.2: Indicator lists feed detection; that is not hunting.
whyNot.3: Handling alerts is triage, a reactive activity.

questions.prompt: How does a SOC most often use MITRE ATT&CK?
choices: To calculate the ALE of attack scenarios
To encrypt and sign its logs before archiving
To certify the skills of its analysts
To map the techniques its rules detect
questions.explanation: ATT&CK describes attackers' tactics and techniques; the SOC uses it to map its detection coverage and guide hunting.

whyNot.0: ALE belongs to quantitative risk analysis.
whyNot.1: ATT&CK has no encryption role.
whyNot.2: ATT&CK is not a certification program.

questions.prompt: Which indicators help steer a SOC? (2 answers)
choices: The false positive rate per rule
MTTR (mean time to respond)
The number of wallpapers deployed
The number of pages in the security policy
questions.explanation: Detection and response times, and the quality of the rules, measure the effectiveness of the SOC.

whyNot.2: This indicator has no link to security.
whyNot.3: The length of a policy does not measure operational effectiveness.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of a playbook for a SOC?
choices: Replacing the SIEM for log collection
Avoiding any escalation to levels 2 and 3
Removing the need to keep logs
Handling each type of alert quickly and consistently
questions.explanation: The playbook describes the checks and actions to carry out: every analyst handles the case the same way, without missing a step.

whyNot.0: The playbook relies on the SIEM; it does not replace it.
whyNot.1: The playbook precisely defines when to escalate.
whyNot.2: Logs remain essential for analysis.

questions.prompt: The EDR reports that a document launched PowerShell, which contacts an unknown address. Which immediate actions are appropriate? (2 answers)
choices: Restart the workstation to clear the memory
Isolate the workstation from the network through the EDR
Close the alert because the user says they did nothing
Search for the same email or file on the other workstations and mailboxes
questions.explanation: Contain by isolating the workstation, then measure the scope by looking for the same indicators elsewhere.

whyNot.0: Restarting erases useful evidence in memory.
whyNot.2: The user usually does not see the malicious execution: their opinion is not enough.

questions.prompt: What is the main danger of alert fatigue?
choices: A real attack drowned in the noise and handled too quickly
Logs too small to be usable
A firewall so strict that it blocks legitimate traffic
A rise in the cost of SIEM licenses
questions.explanation: Overwhelmed analysts skip steps and end up missing a real alert.

whyNot.1: The size of the logs is not the issue.
whyNot.2: Alert fatigue affects analysts, not the firewall.
whyNot.3: Cost is not the main danger.

questions.prompt: In the classification of controls, how is a SOC mainly described?
choices: A purely deterrent control, by its mere presence
A physical control, like a surveillance camera
A purely compensating control, for lack of patches
A detective control, with a corrective part during containment
questions.explanation: The SOC detects incidents and helps correct them by containing them quickly.

whyNot.0: Its presence may deter, but that is not its main role.
whyNot.1: The SOC is a technical and organizational control, not a physical one.
whyNot.2: It can compensate for a weakness, but its primary function is detection.
